`fifo()` vs. processx vs. winpipe

Source: vignettes/compare.Rmd
compare.Rmd

R can talk to Windows named pipes in three ways: base R’s fifo(), processx::conn_create_fifo() and processx::conn_connect_fifo(), and winpipe. They behave quite differently on Windows. This vignette shows what each can and cannot do, using a small external server written in PowerShell as the peer.

library(winpipe)
library(processx)

A test peer

Named pipes live in the \\.\pipe\ namespace. Every pipe on the machine is listed by list.files("//./pipe/"), but the ones that ship with Windows are access controlled, so they make poor examples. Instead, I create a helper function ps_server() that starts a tiny server using the PowerShell. Open the details below to see how it works.

Code for the named pipe helper 
ps_script <- tempfile(fileext = ".ps1")
writeLines('
param($name, $mode, $msg, $log)
$dir = if ($mode -eq "out8" -or $mode -eq "out16") { "Out" }
       elseif ($mode -eq "in") { "In" } else { "InOut" }
$s = New-Object System.IO.Pipes.NamedPipeServerStream($name, [System.IO.Pipes.PipeDirection]::$dir)
$s.WaitForConnection()
if ($mode -eq "out8") {
  $w = New-Object System.IO.StreamWriter($s)
  $w.WriteLine($msg); $w.Flush()
} elseif ($mode -eq "out16") {
  $enc = New-Object System.Text.UnicodeEncoding($false, $false)
  $w = New-Object System.IO.StreamWriter($s, $enc)
  $w.WriteLine($msg); $w.Flush()
} elseif ($mode -eq "echo") {
  $r = New-Object System.IO.StreamReader($s)
  $w = New-Object System.IO.StreamWriter($s)
  $line = $r.ReadLine()
  # The client may already be gone, e.g., if it failed to write
  try { $w.WriteLine("echo: $line"); $w.Flush() } catch {}
} else {
  $r = New-Object System.IO.StreamReader($s)
  $r.ReadLine() | Out-File -Encoding ascii $log
}
Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 1000
$s.Dispose()
', ps_script)

ps_server <- function(name, mode, msg = "", log = "") {
  system2(
    "powershell",
    c("-NoProfile", "-ExecutionPolicy", "Bypass", "-File", shQuote(ps_script),
      name, mode, shQuote(msg), shQuote(log)),
    wait = FALSE
  )
  
  for (i in 1:100) {
    if (name %in% list.files("//./pipe/")) return(invisible())
    Sys.sleep(0.1)
  }
  stop("Pipe '", name, "' was not created")
}

ps_server() starts a server in the background. Its mode decides what it does once a client connects: send a line as UTF-8 ("out8") or UTF-16 ("out16"), read a line ("in"), or echo a line back ("echo").

fifo()

On Unix, fifo() opens a FIFO that you create with mkfifo. On Windows, R implements it with Win32 named pipes, but with different semantics:

  • Opening for reading ("r") connects to an existing pipe as a client.
  • Opening for writing ("w") creates the pipe, i.e., R becomes the server. It cannot connect to a pipe that already exists.
  • Data is read and written as UTF-16, not as bytes.

The last point is easy to miss. If the peer sends ordinary UTF-8 or ASCII text, readLines() returns nothing:

ps_server("demo-fifo-utf8", "out8", "hello from powershell")

con <- fifo("\\\\.\\pipe\\demo-fifo-utf8", "r", blocking = FALSE)
for (i in 1:10) {
  res <- readLines(con)
  if (length(res)) break
  Sys.sleep(0.2)
}
res
#> character(0)
close(con)

The connection opened without error, the server saw the client, but the bytes were decoded as wide characters and discarded. If the peer happens to send UTF-16, the text arrives:

ps_server("demo-fifo-utf16", "out16", "hello from powershell")

con <- fifo("\\\\.\\pipe\\demo-fifo-utf16", "r", blocking = FALSE)
for (i in 1:10) {
  res <- readLines(con)
  if (length(res)) break
  Sys.sleep(0.2)
}
res
#> [1] "hello from powershell"
close(con)

Because "w" creates the pipe, fifo() also cannot write to an existing server. Opening in "r+" mode connects, but writing fails:

ps_server("demo-fifo-echo", "echo")

con <- fifo("\\\\.\\pipe\\demo-fifo-echo", "r+", blocking = FALSE)
try(writeLines("hello", con))
#> Error in writeLines("hello", con) : cannot write to this connection
close(con)

So fifo() can be used between two R processes that both expect UTF-16, but not to talk to an arbitrary program. A request/response protocol such as HTTP is not possible.

processx

processx provides its own connection type that works on both Unix and Windows. The reading end creates a pipe with conn_create_fifo(), and a writer attaches to it with conn_connect_fifo():

reader <- conn_create_fifo()
writer <- conn_connect_fifo(conn_file_name(reader), write = TRUE)

conn_write(writer, "hello\nthere\n")
poll(list(reader), 1000)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "ready"
conn_read_lines(reader, 1)
#> [1] "hello"

close(writer)
#> NULL
close(reader)
#> NULL

It also connects to pipes created by other programs. Unlike fifo(), it reads bytes, so UTF-8 text from our PowerShell server arrives intact:

ps_server("demo-px", "out8", "hello from powershell")

con <- conn_connect_fifo("\\\\?\\pipe\\demo-px", read = TRUE)
poll(list(con), 2000)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "ready"
conn_read_lines(con, 1)
#> [1] "hello from powershell"
close(con)
#> NULL

The limits are in the design:

  • A connection is one-directional. A pipe created by conn_create_fifo() can only be read from, and a connection made with write = TRUE can only write. A request/response exchange over a single pipe does not fit.
  • The connections are processx_connection objects, not R connections. readLines(), read.csv(), writeBin() etc. do not work on them.
  • There is no way to set a security descriptor.

winpipe

winpipe exposes a Win32 named pipe as a native R connection. A client connects with server = FALSE, can read and write on the same pipe, and every R function that accepts a connection works. The echo server demonstrates the request/response exchange:

ps_server("demo-wp-echo", "echo")

con <- winpipe("demo-wp-echo", open = "r+", server = FALSE)
writeLines("hello", con)
Sys.sleep(0.5)
readLines(con)
#> [1] "echo: hello"
close(con)

winpipe also reads UTF-8 from external servers, like processx:

ps_server("demo-wp-out8", "out8", "hello from powershell")

con <- winpipe("demo-wp-out8", open = "r", server = FALSE)
Sys.sleep(0.5)
readLines(con)
#> [1] "hello from powershell"
close(con)

Opening the client with "r" or "w" requests only that access, so it can also connect to one-way pipes such as the processx reader:

reader <- conn_create_fifo()
name <- sub("^\\\\\\\\[.?]\\\\pipe\\\\", "", conn_file_name(reader))

client <- winpipe(name, open = "w", server = FALSE)
writeLines("hello from winpipe", client)

poll(list(reader), 2000)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "ready"
conn_read_lines(reader, 1)
#> [1] "hello from winpipe"

close(client)
close(reader)
#> NULL

winpipe can also be the server, accept clients without blocking the R session, and take a security descriptor. See vignette("basics").

Summary

fifo() processx winpipe
Connection type R connection processx_connection R connection
Platforms Unix and Windows Unix and Windows Windows only
Connect to existing pipe read only yes (one direction) yes
Create a pipe (server) write mode only reading end yes
Bidirectional no no yes
Text encoding on Windows UTF-16 bytes bytes
Talk to non-R programs not reliably one direction yes
Non-blocking yes yes, via poll() yes
Access control (SDDL) no no yes

The behaviour of fifo() and processx described above was observed on Windows with R 4.6 and may differ on other versions.
